units.quote:
This mangrove area was experiencing
substantial shoreline erosion from storms, ship wakes, and
changing hydrodynamic conditions resulting from nearby land
reclamation (Cheong K. H. et al., 2013; Cheong S.-M. et al., 2013).

context.practice_as_described: Mangrove rehabilitation by planting on an eroding shoreline; actually done as hybrid engineering (rock wall, sediment bags, multi-species planting in 8,000 tubes).
context.note: Case description p7 (Pulau Tekong named p6-7). A design judgement that plain planting would fail on an eroding shore - not a measured planting failure; survival of the hybrid planting not reported here. Erosion drivers include ship wakes and land reclamation as well as storms. Same review p8: hybrid engineering is used 'in eroding areas where mangrove planting or natural recruitment would never be successful' - same idea, not emitted twice. The 94% mortality on p7 (ev_establishment_survival_ellison20_1) is Pulau Semakau, not a wave-exposed site.

units.quote:
Dans le scénario IFN, la restauration des mangroves devrait augmenter la productivité de la 
pêche artisanale de 3,0 %. Cette augmentation résulte de l’amélioration des habitats de 
reproduction des juvéniles, de la meilleure santé des écosystèmes et de l’expansion des zones 
de reproduction. (English: In the IFN scenario, mangrove restoration is expected to increase artisanal fishery productivity by 3.0%. This increase results from improved juvenile breeding habitat, better ecosystem health and the expansion of breeding areas. The analysis assumes a 25-year lag to reach this productivity gain, reflecting the gradual recovery of fish populations and the stabilisation of ecosystems. This improvement directly benefits artisanal fishing communities and the women involved in fish processing.)

relationship.outcome_raw: assumed gain in artisanal fishery productivity from mangrove restoration (nursery habitat for juveniles)

context.practice_as_described: Mangrove replanting (207 ha planted 2024-2026) plus conservation management of mangrove protected areas (community heritage areas APAC and marine protected areas, up to 14,996 ha) in Casamance, Senegal, assessed by the IISD Sustainable Asset Valuation (SAVi) model, 2024-2050. Baseline: business-as-usual scenario without the restoration project.
context.note: Annex B p57-58 (PDF p76). Annex B 'Hypothèses de modélisation' of a preliminary ex-ante model report: a hardcoded modelling assumption (design choice), not a measurement. No source cited for the 3.0%. The model applies it to 10% of regional artisanal production (about 6.0 million kg/yr) taken as affected by the intervention area. Food-supply value (+3.0%) and fishery revenue in the executive summary are outputs of this same assumption (not emitted).

units.quote:
Where reforestation was 
successful, land i s  accreting, biodiversity i s  being restored, and farming and other 
economic activities are protected from storms, wind, and salt. In contrast, where 
mangrove seedlings were planted too small, at too shallow a depth, and not carefully 
monitored (to replace plants washed away or dead), the coastline i s  moving inland, 
sweeping away solid ground and endangering the dikes built to protect the resettled areas.

context.note: IEG PPAR (independent, ex-post); 'unless otherwise stated, the PPAR uses ICR data for project achievements while relying on visual observation' (p49). Southern Mekong Delta: Ca Mau, Bac Lieu, Soc Trang, Tra Vinh. Income group from the WB lookup (upper_middle); Vietnam was low / lower-middle income during the project. Evaluator's lessons-section synthesis of the field findings, not a measurement. The failure half is an establishment failure (catalogue #27), not harm. Salt protection: no salinity-intrusion VONT id (gap). Casuarina windbreaks are part of the planting.

units.citation: Wibisono, I.T.C.; Sualia, I. (2008). An Assessment of Lessons Learnt from the Green Coast Project in NAD Province and Nias Island (Period 2005-2008). Wetlands International Indonesia Programme, Bogor.
units.quote:
One real impact of the mangroves was the increased populations of mangrove crabs
(Scyllla serata) and oysters. For example, there was a rapid rise in the incomes of
women oyster gatherers. Before the mangroves were planted, they had had to travel
up to 3 km from the village to find oysters; now they can easily gather the same amount
in the close vicinity of the village. Another example was given in an interview by group
member Pak Ridwan, who pointed out that after planting mangroves as much as 3kg
of crabs could be captured in one night. With a retail price of Rp35,000/kg, the crabs
sell to the market retailers at Peunayong-Banda Aceh market for Rp25,000/kg.

relationship.outcome_raw: mangrove crab and oyster populations and gathering effort after mangrove planting in and around silvo-fishery ponds (oyster gatherers no longer travel up to 3 km; crab catch per night from an interview)

context.practice_as_described: Silvo-fishery (mina tani): mangroves planted on pond dykes, in ponds and along the channels serving traditional tidal aquaculture ponds, about two years before the observation. Baseline: before the mangroves were planted.
context.note: Printed p86 (PDF p101). Anecdotal: one interviewee (crab catch) and a statement about women oyster gatherers; no counts. Grey literature by the implementer (positive-bias risk). Women are the oyster gatherers (gender note). The same page says mangroves along dykes strengthen the embankments (not measured). Harvest and profit figures of the Krueng Tunong silvo-fishery pond (p87) reflect grant-funded aquaculture inputs, not the mangroves, and were not emitted.

units.quote:
Disturbance of the fine sediment balance is a major, yet overlooked, 
root cause of the poor success of rehabilitation efforts on eroding 
coastlines (Winterwerp et al., 2005; Anthony and Gratiot, 2012; Besset 
et al., 2019). In these studies, the changes in sediment dynamics and 
bathymetry, which form the root cause of erosion, were also found to 
prevent mangrove re-establishment, and resumption of their coastal 
protection services.

context.practice_as_described: Mangrove rehabilitation in the Timbulsloko backwater basin (Demak, north coast of Central Java) within a Nature-based Solutions (Building with Nature) project combining coastal engineering (permeable brushwood dams) with ecological recovery; cover regrew 2005-2018 through several planting initiatives plus partial natural recovery. Baseline: the same basin before the fishery developed (no mangrove finfish fishery recorded 2014-2015).
context.note: Discussion p8, drawing on Results p5-7. Supporting data in the same paper (not emitted separately, one dataset one unit): 86% of fishers with more than one year at the site said catch size or quantity had improved (p5, Table 1); lift-net installations counted on satellite images rose 8 (June 2015) to 38 (April 2018) (p7), lagging mangrove recovery. Landscape-level before-after, no replicated control; authors list subsidence and multiple initiatives as alternative explanations (p9) and say many juvenile fish are caught below maturation size (overfishing risk, p6). Fish stock abundance was not measured. COI: co-authors from Wetlands International (Building with Nature implementing partner). About half the fishers came from outside the village.

Site-A = Jiudhara union, Morrelganj, Bagerhat: 'a location in the shadow of mangrove and within a polder' (polder-35/2, embankment 4-5 m). BASELINE = site-B, Bara Bighai union, Patuakhali Sadar: 'a location not in the shadow of mangrove, but within a polder' (polder-43/2, same embankment height). Site-C (no mangrove, no polder) is a grey-infrastructure arm and is NOT the counterfactual used here. 'Polder' = an embanked low-lying area protected by an earthen dyke. 'Shadow of mangrove' = sheltered by the forest from the cyclone's seaward side (p5, Table 1).
context.note: Damage-cost-avoided household survey after super cyclone Sidr (15 Nov 2007; p1 'super cyclone Sidr', p3 'Category IV', 'wind speed up to 240 km/h and produced 6 m of tidal waves'). 300 household heads, 100 per site, 5 villages x 20 households per site; recall survey in Dec 2015, eight years after the event (p12: 'completely based on the memory of the respondents'). Kruskal-Wallis test across all THREE sites (Table 3, p8); no pairwise site-A vs site-B test, so significance left not_reported. Mangrove presence varies at site level only (one site per arm), so unreplicated=true. Confounds named by the authors: site-B about 5 km closer to the cyclone path (Table 1: 30 vs 25 km; p11), sites only 'anecdotally similar' in exposure; authors: 'this study is not enough to conclude with a value' (p12). units.quote:
Seven months after planting, one of the seven mangroves dis­
appeared for unknown reasons. Six plants survived for 31 months in 
good condition; however, after 36 months, withered leaves were 
observed in two of the mangroves. As shown in Fig. 4, Typhoon Haishen 
occurred 16 months after planting, indicating that the typhoon did not 
cause any external damage to the six mangroves.

relationship.outcome_raw: damage to young planted mangroves from a strong typhoon passing near the island 16 months after planting: none of the six surviving plants damaged

context.practice_as_described: PLANTING: seven Kandelia sp. propagules (average 19 cm) planted directly at the seaward (frontal) edge of an existing natural mangrove forest in the innermost part of a calm bay, May 2019; survival and growth monitored for 36 months (p9, p12). No unplanted comparison; the asset outcome is damage/loss of the planted stems during the event.
context.note: Results p9: 7 planted, 1 lost at 7 months for unknown reasons (before the typhoon), 6 survived 31 months; typhoon at 16 months caused no external damage; withered leaves on 2 plants at 36 months. Author caveats (abstract p2, conclusion p12-13): survival was partly FORTUITOUS - peak waves coincided with LOW TIDE and the site is deep inside a sheltered bay where offshore waves were strongly attenuated; modelled oscillatory acceleration of the young plants was ~1 g and would have been ~5 g at higher tide, enough to damage leaves. Author calls it 'a fairly strong typhoon' / 'one of the strongest typhoons of recent years' (p2, p4) - not mapped to a severity class (no inference). n = 6-7 plants, one site, one species: case-study weight. A one-metre Tonga tsunami (2022) also caused no visible damage, again at low tide (p12). Cited background (p3): Philippine plantings long-term survival 10-20% (Primavera & Esteban 2008) - not emitted (establishment survival, not hazard; cited secondary).

context.note: Round-7 decision t3t6r7_mg_carbon (A). Same chronosequence dataset as ev_carbon_sequestration_song23_1 (aboveground biomass stock 127.7 Mg C/ha at 40 years) but a different carbon pool (sediment) and a rate, so emitted separately. Caveats: authors call it 'carbon storage (or preservation)' and 'assuming adequate hydrologic function'; the rate is a derived annual increment of the predicted 40-year stock, which includes carbon present before restoration - p2 says increments after excluding initial sediment storage are still higher than afforestation but shrink with age (Supplementary Fig. 2). The quote's comparison (1.6 Mg C/ha/yr, 65.0 Mg C/ha) is mangrove AFFORESTATION of tidal flats - not this practice (no family; converts mudflat habitat, p5) - so it is not a counterfactual and not encoded. Not emitted (same dataset, #61): total ecosystem stock 232.8-407.0 Mg C/ha over the first 40 years (p2, Fig. 2d); 'reforestation would sequester 60% more carbon per hectare than afforestation' (p4, a pathway-vs-pathway contrast); global potential 671.5-688.8 Tg CO2-eq over 40 years (abstract; a total, no per-ha denominator). Units: Mg C (not CO2); x 3.67 for CO2 - not converted here.
